analysis.one_liner: Charges oil and gas companies a fee on methane they leak into the atmosphere.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after introduction it sat in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee for the rest of the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Treasury Department to measure methane leaking from every oil and gas producing basin and charge each company $1,800 per ton of methane emitted above a small leakage threshold, with the charge rising each year with inflation plus 2%. Companies could lower their bill by measuring their own leaks with independently reviewed methods and fixing them. All the money collected would fund grants to protect coastal communities from storms, flooding, and rising seas.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people benefit twice: cutting methane — a gas that traps 28 to 36 times more heat than carbon dioxide over a century — slows warming, and every dollar of the fee funds coastal resilience grants that protect homes and towns from flooding and storms. Companies that already keep leaks low would gain a relative advantage over leaky competitors, and firms building methane-detection technology would find customers.

how_it_helps.text: Methane is a potent heat-trapping gas responsible for roughly a quarter of observed global warming, and about a third of human-caused methane emissions come from producing and moving fossil fuels, so charging for leaks targets a major driver of climate change [S3].
The fee starts at $1,800 per ton of methane for 2023 and rises each year by 2% plus inflation, giving companies a standing financial reason to find and fix leaks rather than vent or flare gas [S3].
Every dollar collected is transferred annually to the National Coastal Resilience Fund, which pays for projects that protect coasts from storms, flooding, and sea-level rise [S3].

Companies can opt into a lower-cost path by submitting a publicly available, peer-reviewed measurement protocol, installing state-of-the-art leak detection, and ending routine venting and flaring — so the bill rewards cleanup, not just payment [S3].

The bill's findings note that about half of methane emissions from global oil and gas supply chains could be eliminated at zero net cost, meaning much of the reduction would not raise energy costs at all [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies that produce, gather, process, or transmit fuel pay the fee, based on how much methane escapes from their operations and the basins where they work. Some of that cost would likely be passed through to consumers as slightly higher fuel prices, though the bill is designed so companies can cut their bill to near zero by fixing leaks.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies, partly energy consumers

drawbacks.text: The $1,800-per-ton charge would raise operating costs for oil and gas producers, and some share of that would be passed to households through higher prices for natural gas, gasoline, and goods that depend on them — a cost that falls hardest on lower-income households that spend more of their income on energy.

Companies that cannot quickly fix leaks face a steep new bill; the measure could shrink margins for smaller producers and add reporting and compliance burdens, though the escalation is 2% plus inflation rather than an immediate shock beyond the initial rate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is sound on its own terms: methane is one of the fastest ways to slow warming, much of the leakage is technically fixable at little cost, and the money collected funds visible public protection on the coasts. The real cost is modestly higher energy prices where companies pass the fee through, and the design's reliance on accurate basin-level methane measurement — a task the bill assigns to Treasury with satellite and on-the-ground data — would have been a genuine administrative challenge. Weighing a potent climate pollutant against a fee companies could largely avoid by fixing leaks, the benefits outweigh the costs for most people.

outcome.mechanism: It was read once and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on March 9, 2021, with Sens. Cory Booker and Brian Schatz as cosponsors [S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works — the last action it ever received [S5].
No markup, hearing vote, floor vote, or further action appears in the bill's record for the rest of the 117th Congress, which ended January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers are better off: the methane fee never took effect, so no company pays for leaked gas and leaky operators face no penalty. Companies that would have sold leak-detection technology and coastal contractors who would have built resilience projects also lost out.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers dodged the methane fee

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.role: U.S. Senator from Rhode Island; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its methane fee design on March 9, 2021.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; cosponsor

against.name: Sen. Thomas Carper
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a markup or any further consideration of the bill after its referral; the committee record shows no action beyond referral.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral for all Senate environmental bills
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 9, 2021 and took no action on it for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Companies that produce, gather, process, and transmit oil and natural gas
against.what_they_did: The bill placed a direct per-ton charge on their methane emissions, a cost the industry consistently opposed across methane-fee proposals of this era; no industry lobbying appears in the bill's own record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had three Democratic sponsors and no Republican cosponsors, and it died in a Democratic-chaired committee without a vote, so no roll-call ever showed where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and midstream companies
industries.note: The bill charges $1,800 per ton of methane emitted above a 0.2% leakage threshold, rising 2% plus inflation annually — a direct new cost scaled to how much gas each company wastes. Companies that measure and fix their leaks with validated methods can shrink the fee to nearly nothing, so it penalizes sloppy operators specifically.

industries.industry: Methane detection and monitoring technology firms
industries.note: The bill requires companies to use empirically determined, peer-reviewed leak measurement — on the ground or by drone, airplane, or satellite — and rewards installing state-of-the-art detection, creating a customer base for these firms.
All fee revenue flows to the National Coastal Resilience Fund as grants, funding shoreline and flood-protection work performed by restoration and engineering firms.
